report.source_text: Twenty-four hours later, he underwent surgery. An open repair via supra-infraumbilical incision was performed. Intraperitoneal access to the aorta was obtained via dislocation of the colon and small intestine. The lesion was included into a giant omentum sac, and was extremely fragile and hemorrhagic due to the chronic inflammatory process, and a covered rupture was revealed (Figure 4). We found 4 liters of ascites and blood in the peritoneal cavity.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 43-year-old man with a history of splenectomy presented with fever and ascites. Initial CT scan revealed a large amount of free ascites and a giant mass in the left upper-abdominal quadrant, paraaortic and underneath the pancreas. Subsequent CT-angiography confirmed a giant splenic aneurysm (9.8 cm diameter, 5 cm length) with a concomitant arteriovenous shunt, evidenced by contrast infusion into an enlarged splenic vein. A diagnostic centesis was performed, but its results were not documented. Twenty-four hours later, the patient underwent surgery, which revealed the splenic aneurysm to be extremely fragile and hemorrhagic due to a chronic inflammatory process, with a covered rupture. Four liters of ascites and blood were found in the peritoneal cavity.

CT-angio showed concomitant contrast infusion into the enlarged splenic vein, indicating an AV-shunt due to common ligation of vessels after splenectomy and long stump presence.
Surgery revealed the lesion (splenic aneurysm) was extremely fragile and hemorrhagic due to a chronic inflammatory process, with a covered rupture.
During surgery, 4 liters of ascites and blood were found in the peritoneal cavity.
